To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

sleep requirement decreases across mammals and with age in rats, that sleep requirement decreases with a decreasing ratio of cortical neuronal density to surface area, and that the evolution of larger brains and bodies may have been driven by decreasing sleep requirement.

sleep duration decreases across species and during development with decreasing ratio between cortical neuron density and cortical surface area, which causes sleep-inducing metabolic byproducts to accumulate more slowly.

(1) Daily sleep requirement decreases with increasing numbers of cortical brain neurons in mammalian evolution, (2) daily sleep requirement decreases with age in rat development, and (3) both effects are mediated by a decreasing ratio between neuronal density and cortical surface area.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question why mammals sleep less than other animals.
the evolution of sleep and sleep regulation in mammals.
the evolution of sleep and the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

sleep requirement in mammals is determined by a ratio between cortical neuronal surface area and density, that the latter ratio decreases in evolution and development, that the decrease in the ratio leads to a decrease in sleep requirement, and that the decreased sleep requirement then allows for increased feeding hours, which then allows for further increases in brain and body mass.
the evolution of the mammalian brain is driven by a need for increased energy intake, which is facilitated by decreased sleep requirements.

the evolutionary trend of increasing body size and brain mass in mammals was driven by the evolution of a decreased sleep requirement, which in turn was driven by the increasing number of cortical neurons.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
decreasing sleep requirement is a key driver of mammalian evolution.

the evolution of mammals is characterized by increasing body and brain mass, which requires more calories and thus more hours of feeding, and that this trend is driven by increasing numbers of brain neurons, which are coupled to decreasing sleep requirement through a slower accumulation of sleep-inducing metabolite in the parenchyme.
sleep duration is a consequence of the number of neurons, not the other way around.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sleep requirement is not constant across mammals, but rather decreases with increasing numbers of brain neurons, which may have facilitated the increase of body and brain size in mammalian evolution.
the brain has evolved to become larger and more complex by decreasing sleep requirement.
sleep requirement is regulated by the ratio between neuronal density and surface in the cerebral cortex.
